content:
**Quick answer:** Physiotherapy can help some people with arthritis improve movement, muscle strength, fitness and confidence with everyday activity. A physiotherapist assesses how arthritis affects you and develops an activity or exercise approach suited to your symptoms and abilities. It does not cure arthritis or reverse joint changes, and the right programme depends on your condition and individual needs.

## What physiotherapy is, and what it is not

Physiotherapy helps people affected by illness, injury or disability with movement and physical function, and the NHS lists arthritis among the joint and muscle problems it can treat. For arthritis, the focus is usually on helping you move and function as well as possible rather than trying to "fix" the joint.

A physiotherapist may consider your affected joints, movement, muscle strength, balance, walking, daily activities, exercise habits, symptoms, goals and other relevant health conditions. Someone with knee osteoarthritis needs different support from someone managing inflammatory arthritis, hand problems, balance difficulties or recovery after surgery.

## What a physiotherapist can do for arthritis

- Help you understand how to move safely.
- Develop appropriate strengthening exercises.
- Support comfortable joint movement.
- Discuss suitable ways to improve general fitness.
- Assess balance and mobility.
- Help you return gradually to valued activities.
- Advise on adapting exercise when symptoms fluctuate.

## What happens at an appointment

A first appointment usually involves discussing your symptoms, medical history, lifestyle and goals, followed by assessment of relevant physical function such as strength, movement, balance or walking. Expect to cover where you have pain or stiffness, when symptoms are most noticeable, activities you find difficult, walking and stairs, work or hobbies, previous exercise, flare-ups, and what you hope to achieve.

You should be able to tell the physiotherapist if something feels uncomfortable or if you are worried about a movement. Physiotherapy should be collaborative.

## Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis

Physiotherapy is particularly relevant to osteoarthritis because exercise is a core treatment: NICE recommends tailored therapeutic exercise, including local muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness, and supervised therapeutic exercise may also be considered. This does not mean exercise rebuilds cartilage or reverses osteoarthritis; its role is supporting physical function and symptom management.

For rheumatoid arthritis, physiotherapy can form part of supportive care, helping with fitness, muscle strength and joint flexibility. Because RA is an autoimmune inflammatory condition, physiotherapy does not replace the medical treatment used to control the disease. During a flare, activity may need adjusting, and if an activity causes severe pain or joints become warm and swollen, stop rather than forcing through it.

## Will the exercises hurt?

Some movement may feel challenging or unfamiliar, but a "no pain, no gain" approach is not appropriate for arthritis. Tell your physiotherapist if an exercise causes sharp, severe or unusual pain, significant new swelling, or symptoms that repeatedly worsen afterwards. The exercise may simply need changes to its range, resistance, duration or technique.

A useful habit: tell your physiotherapist what happens later in the day or the next morning, not only how an exercise feels during the appointment. If fatigue makes exercise difficult, say so; shorter sessions, additional rest, fewer exercises at one time, spreading activity across the day or choosing a higher-energy time can all help.

A home exercise programme should be realistic. If it feels too difficult, takes too long or consistently aggravates symptoms, discuss it rather than forcing yourself through it. Progress should usually be gradual: avoid suddenly increasing repetitions, resistance, duration, speed and the number of exercises all at once.

## Walking, mobility aids and everyday function

Physiotherapy can be particularly useful if arthritis is changing the way you walk. A physiotherapist may assess your walking pattern, balance, leg strength and confidence, and advise on mobility aids where appropriate; the correct type, height and technique matter. A walking aid is not a failure. For some people, the right equipment makes movement safer or more manageable.

It is also worth knowing the difference between a physiotherapist and an occupational therapist. Physiotherapy tends to focus on movement, strength, exercise, walking, balance and physical function; occupational therapy focuses on everyday activities such as dressing, work tasks, kitchen and household tasks, and equipment and adaptations. The roles can overlap, and some people benefit from both.

## NHS and private access

Physiotherapy is available through the NHS, but access routes vary. In many areas you can self-refer to community musculoskeletal services without a GP referral, and some GP surgeries have first contact physiotherapists who specialise in bone, joint and muscle problems. Availability and pathways differ locally, so check current NHS information for your area.

Private physiotherapy is another option. If you use a private physiotherapist, check that they are registered with the Health and Care Professions Council; you may also see chartered physiotherapists using MCSP after their name.

## How to get more from physiotherapy

- Be clear about your goals: walking to the local shop, playing with grandchildren, gardening, managing stairs, getting out of a chair more comfortably.
- Mention difficult days: what happens during flare-ups and how fatigue affects you.
- Ask if you do not understand an exercise: what you are doing, why, how to adapt it, and what symptoms should make you stop.
- Keep the programme realistic: if you cannot fit it into your day, say so.
- Ask how to change things during a flare, and when to contact the physiotherapist or your GP.

## When joint symptoms need medical assessment

Physiotherapy can be helpful, but not every joint problem should simply be managed by exercising it. Speak to a GP if you have unexplained joint pain, swelling or stiffness that is not settling.

> **When to get help**
>
> Seek urgent medical advice if a joint becomes suddenly very painful and swollen, particularly if it feels hot or you have a fever or feel generally unwell. Seek urgent or emergency care for severe swelling, chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, sudden weakness or numbness, loss of bladder or bowel control, or sudden inability to bear weight after an injury.

## Key takeaways

- Physiotherapy can support movement, muscle strength, fitness and everyday function, but it does not cure arthritis or reverse joint changes.
- Exercise is a core part of osteoarthritis management; physiotherapy supports rheumatoid arthritis care alongside medical treatment.
- Start exercises gently, build gradually, and tell your physiotherapist about flare-ups and fatigue.
- NHS physiotherapy access varies by area; self-referral is available in many places.
- A severe, hot or suddenly swollen joint needs appropriate medical assessment, not just exercise.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can physiotherapy cure arthritis?

No. Physiotherapy does not cure arthritis. It can form part of a wider management plan designed to support movement, physical function and symptom management.

### Can I get arthritis physiotherapy on the NHS?

Physiotherapy is available through the NHS. Access routes vary, and self-referral to musculoskeletal services is available in many areas. Check current local NHS information.

### How long does physiotherapy take to work?

There is no reliable single timeframe. Progress depends on your condition, symptoms, goals, programme and individual circumstances.

### What if physiotherapy exercises make my arthritis worse?

Stop or reduce an exercise if it causes sharp, severe or unusual pain, and discuss repeated worsening with your physiotherapist. Your programme may need adjustment.

## A gentle next step

Physiotherapy for arthritis is not about pushing painful joints as hard as possible. It is about finding practical ways to support movement, strength and everyday function at a level appropriate for you. If arthritis is making walking, exercise or daily activities increasingly difficult, consider discussing physiotherapy with your GP, healthcare team or local NHS musculoskeletal service. You can also explore practical arthritis information and support from Living With Arthritis.
